opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that when you're doing adversarial work, the thing you most want to avoid is fooling yourself. Every time you add complexity to an objective, you're adding more places where something can quietly go wrong. Maybe a term in the loss is masking gradients, or two components fight each other, or you've tuned some weighting coefficient until it happens to look good on your evaluation. Then you get a result that looks like progress, and it's not clear whether the model got more robust or whether you just made the optimization harder for the attacker.

With a simple objective, say, maximize the loss within some epsilon ball, or the margin between the correct class and the next most likely one, you can actually reason about what's happening. If the attack fails, you can ask why. Is the loss surface weird? Are the gradients broken? Is the model genuinely robust? You can diagnose it. With a complicated objective, you often can't tell those apart.

There's also a historical lesson here. A lot of the defenses that were later broken had elaborate machinery, and when you looked closely, the robustness came from making gradient-based attacks fail, not from the model being correct on those inputs. The defenses that held up, like standard adversarial training with PGD, are almost embarrassingly simple. That suggests simplicity is correlated with things that actually work, not just things that look like they work.

And practically, simple things compose better. If I have a clean objective, I can swap in a stronger optimizer, change the threat model, or scale up, and I roughly know what to expect. Clever objectives tend to be brittle in ways that only show up later.

So it's not that complexity is always bad. It's that the burden of proof should be much higher. If you add something, you should be able to show why it's necessary, and show you haven't just made evaluation harder.

r001.rationale: The response says simple objectives make failures easier to diagnose by clarifying whether the issue is the loss surface, gradients, or genuine robustness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is that I've been burned so many times by complexity hiding the thing that's actually going wrong. When you have a clean objective, like just the cross-entropy on PGD-generated examples, and the model is robust, you can say with some confidence why it's robust. When it isn't robust, you can usually figure out which assumption failed. The moment you start stacking on extra regularizers, auxiliary losses, clever weighting schemes, you lose that. Every added term is another place for a bug to live, and more importantly, another place for the evaluation to quietly go wrong.

And that last part is really the thing I care about. My whole career has basically been showing that defenses which looked good were actually just confusing the attack rather than stopping it. Almost every time, the failure traced back to some component that made the optimization landscape harder to search, not harder to exploit. Obfuscated gradients, numerically unstable losses, non-differentiable pieces. A simple objective is much harder to accidentally break in that way. If I attack a model trained on a simple loss and the attack fails, I'm more inclined to believe the robustness is real, because there are fewer mechanisms by which I could have fooled myself.

There's also a sort of scientific hygiene argument. With a simple objective, the comparison between methods is meaningful. If you tell me your method gets three points better, and your method has seven moving parts, I don't know which one mattered, and I'm pretty sure neither do you. If the whole thing is one loss and one attack, we can actually have a conversation about what's going on.

I'd add that simplicity isn't the goal in itself. If something complicated genuinely worked and held up under adaptive attacks, I'd be thrilled. It's just that in practice, the simple baselines have aged remarkably well, and most of the complicated things have aged badly, so my prior has shifted accordingly.

r001.rationale: The response says simple objectives make it easier to identify which assumption failed and leave fewer places for bugs, explaining why they can perform well in adversarial training.

astra-6.text:
I tend to like simple objectives because I want to understand what it is that we're actually optimizing. In adversarial training, the goal is fairly straightforward: find an input that causes the model to make a mistake, and then train the model to get that input right. The optimization can be difficult, but the objective doesn't necessarily have to be complicated.

When you add a lot of extra terms, you create more opportunities for the objective to improve without the model becoming more robust. You also make it harder to figure out why something worked. So I prefer to start with the simplest thing that captures the behavior we want, attack it carefully, and add complexity when there's a concrete failure that requires it.

r001.rationale: The response says simpler objectives make it easier to understand what worked, but does not identify ease of debugging as a reason simple loss functions tend to perform well in adversarial training.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to prefer simple objectives because, when something works, I want to understand why it works. In adversarial training, you already have this complicated interaction between the model and the attack you’re using to train it. If you add a bunch of extra loss terms, each with its own coefficient, it becomes very difficult to tell what’s actually responsible for the robustness.

And there’s a particular danger here: you can make the attack’s job harder without making the model more robust. So an objective can look successful because the attack you’re evaluating against fails to find the problems that are still there. A simple objective doesn’t eliminate that risk, but it makes the whole thing easier to analyze and debug.

If a more complicated objective gives you a real improvement under strong evaluation, great. I just want to establish the simple baseline first and make sure the extra complexity is buying us something.

r001.rationale: The response says simple objectives are easier to analyze and debug, making it easier to understand what drives robustness in adversarial training.
